1.pericope_label: After the death of the two sons: the priest’s preparation

schools.summary: Gill offers two placements for the law, either immediately after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, in which case the chapter would stand next to the tenth, or after the intervening rules on uncleanness which were meant to keep defiled worshippers out of the tabernacle, citing Aben Ezra for the view that God cautioned Aaron once he had cautioned the people; he notes that the high priest entered only after the daily morning sacrifice had been offered and the ordinary service performed. Calvin puts the restriction on entry down to the danger of familiarity, since a priest going in promiscuously at every sacrifice would have worn away no small part of the reverence due to the place, and adds that a rite seen only once at the year's end represented the one perpetual sacrifice more clearly; on the vestments he looks past the garments to the office, arguing that a mediator between God and men should be free from every stain, and that since no mortal could supply this a type was substituted, from which believers might learn to expect another.

Henry dates the law after the death of Aaron's two sons and reads it as meeting Aaron's fear that guilt might cleave to his house, or that some later sin of his remaining sons might ruin it, observing that the atonement made for a family is the establishment of it and preserves the entail of blessing upon it. He adds that the priests, warned by those deaths to approach with reverence and godly fear, are here shown how the nearest approach might be made not merely without peril but to unspeakable comfort.

Clarke explains that the holy place here means the innermost division behind the veil, that entry was restricted to the one day in ordinary cases, but that in extraordinary ones the high priest went in more often — in the wilderness to take down and adjust the furniture at every encampment, and on pressing public occasions to consult the Lord. He takes the bullock to cover the high priest, his family, the whole priesthood and probably the Levites, reads the ram as a token that he and his associates were wholly consecrated to the work, and interprets the plain linen as humiliation, since the robe, ephod, breastplate and mitre are all absent, so that a man who elsewhere ministers in his dress of dignity as a representative of Christ here appears before God as a sinner. Wesley gives the same two exceptions to the rule of entry in almost the same words, notes that what went within was the blood while the body was burnt outside, and calls the day one not of feasting but of mourning, when ornaments were laid aside.

Keil and Delitzsch ground the institution in what the daily rites could not do, since many sins would remain unacknowledged and so unexpiated, leaving the congregation with a sense of separation from God and no true joyousness of access; they also fix the force of the opening words, that only with the prescribed sacrifices, dress and purifications could the priest come in at all. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the other end, making the chapter an appropriate close to the laws of purification and an annual supplement completing what was daily practised; he explains that the bullock had to be bought with the priest's own money, a victim expiating his own sins needing to be his own property; and he treats the four white articles as a fixed class of vestment set against the golden garments, noting two sets of differing costliness, an allowance of thirty minae from the community which the priest might supplement himself, and the later practice by which the Sanhedrin sequestered him for seven days beforehand in a Temple chamber, apart from his wife, lest he contract defilement.

debates: When and why the law stands here. Gill leaves the dating open between an immediate sequel to the deaths and a later placement after the purity rules; Ellicott treats the position as deliberate, the day completing the laws of purification; Keil and Delitzsch justify it from the insufficiency of the daily rites to reach unacknowledged sin.

Whether the high priest entered the innermost place only once a year. Clarke and Wesley both allow extraordinary entries, to strike the tabernacle on the march and to consult God on pressing occasions; Calvin treats the single annual entry as the whole point, since frequency would have bred indifference and obscured the type.

Why the priest wore plain linen. Clarke and Wesley make it humiliation, the man appearing as a sinner rather than in his dress of dignity; Ellicott treats it as a defined class of vestment with its own rules and costs; Calvin sees in the change of dress a type of a mediator free from stain.
outliers: Ellicott's report that the Sanhedrin sequestered the high priest for seven days beforehand, lodging him in a Temple chamber away from his wife.
Ellicott's note that the community allowed thirty minae toward the linen vestments, which the priest might supplement from his own money.
Clarke's observation that the high priest's ordinary robes mark him as a representative of Christ, but that on this day he comes as a sinner and dresses accordingly.
Calvin's reason for the single annual entry, that a more frequent one would have worn away the reverence due to the place.
themes: after the death of the two sons
a victim bought with his own money

5.pericope_label: The two goats, the lot, and the blood within the veil

schools.summary: Gill insists that the bullock was the high priest's own, bought at his own expense rather than out of the congregation's funds, since it expiated his own sin, and observes that the high priest had to do only with the congregation of Israel as Christ has to do only with the elect. He sets out the staging of the lots from the Mishnah, with the priest east of the court and north of the altar, his deputy at his right hand and the chief of the fathers' house at his left, and the lots drawn from an urn; he finds the goat an apt emblem on several counts, clean and fit for food and comely in its going, and then on a further count that is not flattering, since something in it is rank and offensive, which suited a surety bearing imputed sin in the likeness of sinful flesh; he notes from Josephus and the Mishnah that the censer was golden on this day where on others the coals were lifted with silver; he records that the Sadducees held the incense was kindled outside the veil, so that the Sanhedrin's messengers put the high priest on oath in the house where the incense was compounded; and he describes another priest keeping the bullock's blood in motion so that it should not congeal. Calvin describes a twofold mode of expiation, one goat offered by the rule of the law and the other sent away as an outcast and offscouring, and fixes on the reason given for the covering cloud, that the priest die not, taking it as a sign of how formidable the divine majesty is, fatal to the sight even of the man who serves it.

Henry reports the Jewish tradition that the high priest withdrew for seven days beforehand, performing the inferior priests' work himself so as to get his hand in, and hearing the institution read over to him again and again; he describes the day beginning very early with the usual morning sacrifice, the whole body washed before dressing and the hands and feet again afterwards, the daily incense burnt and the lamps dressed before the special service began.

Clarke argues that the two goats made a single sacrifice though only one was killed, since no one animal could show both natures of Christ or both his death and his rising, a slain goat not being capable of being made alive again; he reports that one lot bore the Name which the Jews will neither write nor pronounce and the other the word rendered scapegoat, and that the priest put both hands into the urn and drew one in each; and on the disputed word he derives it from goat and dismiss, making it simply the animal sent away, gathering pagan parallels of transferred guilt, chiefly the Egyptian bull whose severed head was loaded with execrations and then sold to Greeks or thrown into the Nile. Wesley divides the two goats the same way as Clarke, one figuring the passion and the other the resurrection, and adds that the eastward face of the priest at the sprinkling signified that he stood there for the people, God being merciful to sinners only through the blood.

Ellicott explains that the two goats and the ram were bought some time earlier out of public money, that under the second Temple the pair had to match in value, size and colour, and that if one died after the lot had fallen a fresh pair was bought while the survivor was kept and fed until ritually defective, then sold for the treasury; he corrects the verb used of the bullock, since the priest only presents or brings it near, the killing coming later, and notes that as a sacrifice for himself he had to slaughter it personally like any layman. He traces the lot-tablets from box or ebony to gold in the later Temple, notes the red thread tied at the neck of one goat and the scarlet thread on the head or horns of the other, reads the disputed word as a proper name throughout, and takes the atonement made with that goat to mean atonement made for it, fitting the beast for what it had to do. He also describes the priest staying within until the place was full of smoke, leaving backward with his face to the sanctuary, praying on emerging that a year meant for drought might be one of rain and that travellers' prayers for fair weather might not be heard, and reports that the sprinklings were counted aloud, one upward and seven downward, lest he lose his place. Keil and Delitzsch keep the same order, the goats set before the Lord and the lots cast over them before anything is slain.

debates: What the disputed word for the second goat means. Clarke derives it from goat and dismiss, so that it names the animal sent away, and supports the sense with pagan parallels of guilt transferred to a victim; Ellicott takes it as a proper name throughout, rendering the lot as for Azazel and the sending as to Azazel, and reads the atonement as made for the goat rather than by it.

Where the incense was kindled. Gill reports that the Sadducees held it was set alight outside the veil, and that the Sanhedrin's messengers therefore put the high priest on oath in the house where the incense was compounded not to vary from their instructions; the rest write throughout as though it was kindled within.

What the pair of goats signifies. Clarke holds that one animal could not have shown both natures and both the death and the rising, so two were needed for one sacrifice; Wesley divides them between the passion and the resurrection; Calvin describes instead a twofold mode of expiation, sacrifice on the one hand and outcasting on the other.
outliers: Ellicott's rule that if one goat died after the lot had fallen a new pair was bought, the survivor being fed until ritually defective and then sold for the treasury.
Gill's account of the oath administered to the high priest in the house where the incense was made, because the Sadducees disputed where it should be kindled.
Ellicott's report of the prayer said on emerging from the veil, that a year meant for drought might be one of rain and that travellers' prayers for fair weather might go unheard.
Ellicott's note that the priest counted the sprinklings aloud lest he lose his place.
themes: a cloud that hides the mercy seat

15.pericope_label: The goat killed, and the holy things cleansed

schools.summary: Gill explains that the holy place here means the innermost, as Aben Ezra says, and that although the Targum adds a verbal confession, atonement was made by blood and not by words; he records how completely the sanctuary was cleared, no priest in the holy place or in any court and none of the people anywhere; and he lays out both parties in the dispute over the altar, the Mishnah with Jarchi and Ben Gersom taking it for the golden altar of incense, which the law elsewhere requires to be atoned for once a year, against Aben Ezra and Bishop Patrick, who read the priest's going out as a departure from the sanctuary where that altar stood and so prefer the altar of burnt offering. On the sprinkling he specifies the right forefinger, seven times, upon a place swept clear of coals and ashes so that the gold showed. Calvin raises the difficulty that a sanctuary God had consecrated should need cleansing at all, since God remains true though all the world be unholy, and answers that the place contracted no defilement in itself yet is justly reckoned unclean in regard to the guilt of the people, drawing from this that sin is thereby made more exceeding sinful, men profaning the sacred name even while meaning to serve it if they serve carelessly; and he reads the clearing of the tabernacle as a temporary banishment felt as punishment, a melancholy sight when those for whom the tent was pitched had to desert it, teaching them that every part of salvation depends on mercy alone.

Henry follows the priest out to kill the people's goat and back in a third time, sprinkling its blood as he had the bullock's, and explains the object: the people's sins had provoked God to withdraw the tokens of his favourable presence, and atonement was made so that, being reconciled, he might continue with them; he then has the same done for the outward part of the tabernacle as for the inner room.

Wesley qualifies the familiar formula about entering once a year, since the priest entered once a year in the sense of one day in the year, though he went in and came out more than once upon that day; he observes that the people never entered that place but their sins entered it, so that the tabernacle needed cleansing merely for standing in the midst of them, and that God thereby showed how much their hearts needed purifying; he adds that the clearing of the sanctuary was for the greater reverence of the divine majesty and to prevent anyone casting an eye into the holy of holies as the priest went in or out; he takes the altar cleansed to be that of incense; and he reads the sevenfold sprinkling as signifying a perfect cleansing and a perfect reconciliation by blood.

Ellicott fills in the second-Temple practice, the vessel set on a golden stand prepared for the purpose, the goat killed on the north side of the altar, the blood caught in a bowl, and the same posture and counted sprinklings repeated on the third entry; he reports that the blood of bullock and goat was afterwards mixed and the court and altar sprinkled eight times with the mixture. From the priest's solitude he draws a historical consequence, that because no one could watch what he did inside, the chief priests and the elders swore him on the eve to alter nothing in the traditional ceremonies. He follows the second-Temple authorities for the altar of incense, gives the order of the corners as north-east, north-west, south-west and south-east, and notes that the blood remaining was poured out where a pipe carried it away to the Kidron. Keil and Delitzsch ground the defilement of the holy things in the body, holding that they were made unclean not merely by the sins of those who touched them but by the bodily manifestations of a nation's sin; they expressly reject Knobel's reason for the empty sanctuary, that none but the chief servant was worthy to be present, holding instead that no unholy person should defile a place just cleansed; and they place the altar rite at the altar in the court.

debates: Which altar was cleansed with the mingled blood. Gill sets the Mishnah, Jarchi and Ben Gersom, who take it for the golden altar of incense, against Aben Ezra and Bishop Patrick, who argue from the priest's going out that the altar of burnt offering is meant; Ellicott and Wesley follow the first party, Keil and Delitzsch the second.

Why no one might be present. Keil and Delitzsch reject by name Knobel's explanation that only the chief servant was worthy, and substitute the danger of an unholy presence defiling a sanctuary just cleansed; Ellicott makes it a precaution against unwitting defilement; Calvin treats it as a banishment meant to be felt; Wesley adds reverence and the prevention of prying.

How a consecrated place can be defiled at all. Calvin raises the objection himself and answers that the sanctuary is unclean in respect of the people's guilt though not in itself; Keil and Delitzsch locate the defilement in the bodily manifestations of national sin; Wesley says only that their sins entered where the people could not.
outliers: Ellicott's account of the oath sworn on the eve by the chief priests and elders, which arose precisely because no one could watch the priest inside.
Ellicott's note that the blood left over ran off by a pipe into the Kidron.
Calvin's remark that men profane the sacred name even while intending to serve it, if they serve carelessly or irreverently.
Keil and Delitzsch's explicit rejection of Knobel's explanation for the emptying of the sanctuary.

20.pericope_label: The scapegoat sent away, and the sin offerings burnt

schools.summary: Gill observes that the goat went where it would never be seen and from whence it would never return, and settles the disputed name against the English version, insisting flatly that the goat and Azazel are two things and not one and are wrongly confounded in the translation. He treats the following verse as describing a fourth entry, made to fetch out the censer and the incense cup, and reports the rabbinic judgment that the whole section stands in order except this verse; he records that the washing was done on the roof of a chamber where fine linen was spread for the priest, and observes that if our Lord was baptized on this day, his baptism being by dipping, type and antitype would answer closely. Calvin calls the sending away the only bloodless sacrifice, yet one not to be separated from the slaying of its fellow as regards efficacy, and turns the defilement of the man who led it into an argument: when the people saw a man shut out of the camp for merely touching the goat, they were forced to reckon how much wider the alienation must be between God and those whose own sin the creature carried.

Henry notes that hands laid on a victim's head were always accompanied by confession, the nature of the confession following the nature of the sacrifice, and remarks that although the later synagogue supplied the high priest with a set form, God prescribed none here, a man so acquainted with his people's state and so concerned for them needing no words found for him; he supposes the blood that remained was poured out at the foot of the brazen altar.

Clarke works through the three nouns of the confession — one from a root meaning to pervert or turn aside, one from a root meaning to rebel, and one from a root meaning to miss the mark — which the Jews took to exhaust every breach of the divine law, and cites the form given by Maimonides; he notes that not only the man who led the goat away but the priest who had consecrated it were reckoned defiled, the animal being unclean as bearing the sins of the whole congregation. Wesley reads the same triple as covering sins of every size, so that the smallest needed and the greatest were not excluded from the benefit represented, and then makes a claim of his own, that the heathen custom of loading one beast or man with a people's curses was taken from this rite rather than merely parallel to it; he also argues that the garments resumed afterwards are the proper high-priestly ones and not the plain linen, partly because the meaner attire suited the humbling and partly because hands laid on the sin-laden goat had in some sort defiled what was worn.

Ellicott observes that the doubled phrase, both his hands, occurs in no other ceremony, and takes it as the most solemn possible sign that the animal stood for priesthood and laity together, adding that the confession was extempore at first and formulated only later. He renders the destination literally as a land cut off, ground separated from all around it, a peak or precipice standing by itself, and glosses the wilderness as uninhabited but reckoned the abode of evil spirits; he then marks how far practice diverged from the text, since the law says only that the goat is to be let go whereas the second-Temple authorities decreed it must be destroyed, a priest leading it some twelve miles to a rock with ten booths built at intervals along the road. He confirms that the two closing acts were performed in the reverse of the written order, the burnt offerings coming first in the golden garments and the white robes resumed only to fetch the censer, and notes that the messenger waited out the day in the last booth, a mile from the city, until sundown. Keil and Delitzsch say the same of those who burned the carcases outside the camp, defiled as they were by animals laden with sin.

debates: What the disputed name denotes. Gill states flatly that the goat and Azazel are two things and not one, and that the English version wrongly confounds them, which puts him with Ellicott's reading of the word as a proper name and against the derivation that makes it merely the goat that departs.

Where the heathen scapegoat customs came from. Wesley derives them directly from this rite, holding that the nations took their practice of loading one beast or man with a people's curses out of it; Clarke treats such customs as parallels found among most ancient nations without deriving them from Israel.

Whether these verses stand in the order performed. Gill reports the rabbis holding the whole section in order except this one verse, which they place later; Ellicott confirms from second-Temple practice that the burnt offerings came first and the white robes were resumed only for the last errand; Wesley reads the change of garments accordingly.
outliers: Ellicott's account of the later decree that the goat be destroyed at a rock some twelve miles out, with ten booths built along the road.
Wesley's claim that the heathen rites of loading a victim with a people's curses were taken from this ceremony.
Gill's conjecture that if our Lord was baptized on this day, type and antitype would answer closely, his baptism being by dipping.
Calvin's argument that a man defiled by merely touching the goat showed how much wider the alienation was between God and those whose sin it carried.
themes: both hands on a living head
a fourth entry, out of order

29.pericope_label: The statute for ever: the tenth day of the seventh month

schools.summary: Gill holds that the word priest is rightly supplied in the clause about making atonement, following Aben Ezra, since no one else could offer a sacrifice and on this day none but the high priest; he reads the sabbath of rest as typical of a cessation from sinful works and from dependence on works of righteousness, notes that only the eldest son was anointed to succeed, takes the threefold statement of the statute as showing a law of considerable moment, and reads the closing sentence with the Targum and the rabbis as saying that Aaron, when the day came, did according to this order. Calvin reads the fast as meant to drive the people into more serious penitential meditation without letting them doubt they were truly purged, insists it worked in a sacramental manner, the outward ceremony being an unmistakable sign of a reconciliation still to come, and takes the emphasis laid on the priest's office as a eulogy of the coming Mediator meant to turn the minds of believers to him alone.

Henry notes that the seventh month had itself been reckoned the first until the exodus displaced it, and reports two guesses at what anniversary the tenth day marked: that it was the day our first parents fell, kept as a fast in memory of the fall, or, as Dr Lightfoot computed, the day Moses came down the last time with the renewed tables and a shining face, which would make a day of forgiveness the fittest date for a day of atonement.

Clarke observes that the parallel law calls the day the ninth at even because the Jewish day began in the evening, notes the additional sacrifices prescribed elsewhere, records that the jubilee trumpet was sounded on this same tenth day every fiftieth year, and identifies the month as Tishri, the seventh of the sacred and the first of the civil year, answering to part of September and October. Wesley finds a plainer convenience in the season, the fruits being all gathered and the people most at leisure, and takes it as God condescending to their necessities; he divides the affliction between body and mind, abstinence from food and other delights on the one hand and grief for former sins on the other, and insists the bitterness is voluntary in every true penitent, which is why they are said to afflict themselves rather than to be afflicted.

Ellicott establishes from the prophets that to afflict the soul means to fast and complains that the Authorised Version renders the same idiom elsewhere as humbling the soul, so that an English reader cannot see it is one phrase; he sets the day in its month among the Feast of Trumpets and the Feast of Tabernacles. He notes that the Hebrew leaves open who makes the atonement, the Lord or the high priest, and prefers the priest; he reports the rule administered in the time of Christ that only sins against God were covered, wrongs to a neighbour requiring that the neighbour be satisfied first, and that a man who sins in the expectation of absolution on this day receives none. He takes the rest commanded as a sabbath of sabbaths, a day of complete rest, observing that the doubled phrase is used of the weekly sabbath, this day and the sabbatical year but of no other festival; he reports that hereditary right to the high priesthood was held conditional in a way property is not, the son succeeding only if morally and physically blameless with the elders judging his fitness; and he marks a translator's inconsistency at the close, one Hebrew phrase standing three times within four verses and being Englished two ways. Keil and Delitzsch hold that the very need to repeat the atonement yearly showed the sacrifices of the law insufficient to perfect the servant of God in his own conscience.

debates: What anniversary the tenth day marked. Henry canvasses the fancy that it was the day of the fall of our first parents and Lightfoot's computation that it was the day Moses returned with the renewed tables; Clarke declines the question and fixes the day by the calendar instead, noting the evening reckoning and the jubilee trumpet.

Who makes the atonement in the clause about that day. Ellicott holds the Hebrew ambiguous between the Lord and the high priest and prefers the priest, since he is named a few verses before; Gill treats the supplement as certain, following Aben Ezra, on the ground that none but a priest could offer.

How far the day's cleansing reached. Ellicott reports the rule that only sins against God were covered, a wrong to a neighbour needing his pardon first, and that presumption on the day forfeited its benefit; Keil and Delitzsch limit it differently, taking the annual repetition itself as evidence that these sacrifices could not perfect the conscience.
outliers: Ellicott's report of the rule that a man who sins in the expectation of being absolved on this day is not absolved.
Ellicott's account of the high priesthood as a conditional inheritance, the elders judging whether an heir was morally and physically fit to succeed.
Henry's two rival identifications of the day, the fall of our first parents and Lightfoot's date for the return with the renewed tables.
Ellicott's complaint that one thrice-repeated Hebrew phrase is Englished in two different ways within four verses.
themes: the tenth day of the seventh month
what the day did not cover
